At 5:17 every morning, the town of Bellwether forgot one thing. On Monday it forgot the color blue; by breakfast, people stared at the sky with eyes and called it “that upper shade.” On Tuesday it forgot spoons, and soup became a humiliation. Wednesdays were unpredictable. Once, everyone forgot the word for sleep. Another time, no one could remember how to wink. The forgetting lasted until sunset, when the lost item returned with the pop of a cork leaving a bottle. Nobody knew why. Nobody except Mara, who woke every dawn with a notebook under her pillow and a sentence written inside.

Today the notebook said: Do not let them ring the seventh bell. Mara read it while her brother, Ivo, stood in the kitchen holding a fork his cereal. “What is this?” he asked. “A rake?” Bellwether had forgotten forks. Their mother had tied two pencils with string and was attempting to eat eggs. Beyond the window, the clocktower loomed over the market, its six bells silent in their niches. A seventh niche, high and empty, had puzzled Mara. At noon, Mayor Vale would unveil the town’s restored bell, recovered from the river after seventy years. Mara closed her notebook and ran.

She found her friend Seln repairing bicycles outside the bakery. Seln had remembered forks; he was using one to tighten a screw. “The seventh bell,” Mara said. “We have to stop it.” Seln considered this, then nodded, because Mara’s warnings had a record. Last winter she had predicted the forgetting of doors, and they had spent a day walking through walls that insisted were not there. They crossed the market, past vendors selling versions of everything. At the fountain, Mayor Vale rehearsed his speech beside a velvet object. The river bell was green, and marked with an emblem Mara recognized: an open eye beneath a crescent moon.

Mara had seen the emblem in her grandmother’s attic, stamped on a map whose edges had away. Her grandmother called it the Keepers, then refused to say more. “Mayor Vale,” Mara shouted, pushing through the crowd, “where did you get it?” Vale smiled with the patience reserved for children. “From the riverbed.” “It must not ring.” The smile narrowed. Around them, six clocktower bells began their chime. One. Two. Three. Each note shook dust from awnings. At six, the river bell answered from beneath its cloth. Its sound was low, vast, and wrong. Every person in the square forgot their name.

The panic was brief, then. People pointed at themselves, demanded introductions, and accused of impersonation. Ivo stood beside Mara, but delighted. “I’m somebody,” he announced. “Important.” Mara gripped Seln’s sleeve. He looked at her. “Sorry,” he said. “Do I know you?” The forgetting changed shape. It was no a object or word; it had reached inward. Mayor Vale stared at the uncovered bell with an expression of recognition. “Ah,” he murmured. “So that is what it takes.” He climbed the fountain rim, raised hands, and called for silence. “Good citizens,” he said, “we have been given a chance to begin again.”

Mara heard the notebook rustle in her pocket. She opened it. The page held a map of the square and line of ink leading from the bell to the clocktower’s niche. Beneath it appeared words: A keeper must remember what others cannot. Seln was studying face, trying to place it. Mara wanted to cry, but was to do. She seized Ivo’s hand and ran toward the tower. Behind them, Vale’s speech applause. He promised histories, debts, and freedom from old griefs. The crowd cheered, though people looked uncertain, as if they had misplaced something and were not to know what.

The tower door was locked, which was fortunate: today Bellwether remembered locks. Mara climbed the drainpipe, scraped her knees, and pulled Seln and Ivo through a narrow window. Inside, gears turned with indifference. Six bell ropes hung in a row. A seventh rope, threaded and dark with river water, ran upward through the ceiling. “Cut it,” Mara told Ivo. “With what?” He held up the rake. Seln found an axe for splitting kindling and swung it hard. The rope parted. Below, the river bell gave a groan. Then the tower shuddered, and the empty niche above them filled with moonlight.

For breath, no sound existed. Then the six bells rang backward. Their notes poured into the river bell, pulling a shimmer from its mouth. Mara saw memories: a woman teaching a child to braid hair, a soldier returning without his hand, Ivo at four asleep beneath a quilt. The shimmer rose like smoke and entered the niche. Far below, the crowd gasped. Names returned first. Then forks. Then all the absences Bellwether had endured for came rushing home: lost recipes, vanished songs, forgotten apologies, the names of dead dogs. People fell to their knees, laughing and weeping amid the market stalls.

Mayor Vale did not kneel. He stood in the fountain, to his ankles, looking than Mara had seen him. “You don’t understand,” he said she descended. “Remembering is a weight.” Mara thought of grandmother, who carried the keeper’s map. She thought of all the town’s vanishings, mercies had become theft. “Yes,” Mara said. “That’s why we carry it.” Vale looked the clocktower. In the niche, the shimmer hardened into a silver bell. It ring. It waited. Seln came to Mara’s side, recognition in his eyes. “There you are,” he said. Ivo hugged, asked whether anyone knew forks had gone.

That night, Mara placed the notebook on the windowsill. The page was blank. When she opened it, she found warning, only a question: What will you remember today? Outside, Bellwether stirred beneath a blue sky. Blue, Mara thought, savoring the certainty of it. Down the street, someone dropped a spoon and cursed. Someone began singing a song that had missing for years. At the tower, the silver bell caught the sun. Mara could feel its attention, not sacrifice, merely asking company. She took her notebook, her brother’s hand, and Seln’s sleeve. Together they walked into town, carrying everything they could.
